entry: Algebraic operation on two equal-length sequences of numbers, usually coordinate vectors. The dot product is the sum of the products of corresponding entries; for the vectors [1, 3, −5] and [4, −2, −1] it equals 3. Geometrically, it is the product of the two vectors' lengths and the cosine of the angle between them, and the two definitions agree in [[Cartesian coordinate system|Cartesian coordinates]]. In modern [[Euclidean geometry]], lengths and angles are defined through it: a vector's length is the square root of its dot product with itself. The name derives from the dot operator (⋅) used to write it. The alternative name scalar product stresses that the result is a scalar rather than a vector, as with the [[Cross product|vector product]] in [[Three-dimensional space]].

Port city, largest city and economic capital of Cameroon (pop., 2025: 3,816,500), on the estuary of the Wouri River on the [[Atlantic Ocean|Atlantic]] coast. It handles most of Cameroon's major exports, including oil, cocoa, coffee, timber, metals and fruits, and was home to Central Africa's largest port. The city was a center of the [[Atlantic slave trade|transatlantic slave trade]] in the 18th century and a German protectorate from 1884 to 1895. When Cameroon became independent in 1960, its capital was [[Yaoundé]] and Douala became the major economic city. In 1991 a civil disobedience campaign, the ghost town operation (*ville morte*), shut down economic activity to press for multi-party democracy.

Largest and lowest-pitched [[String instrument|string instrument]] in the modern [[Orchestra|symphony orchestra]]. It has four or five strings, tuned in fourths (usually E1, A1, D2 and G2) rather than in the fifths of the [[Violin]] family, making it the only modern bowed string instrument so tuned. It is a standard member of the orchestra's string section and is featured in [[Concerto|concertos]] and [[Chamber music|chamber music]] in Western [[Classical music|classical music]]. It is also used in jazz, blues, rock and roll and country music, where pizzicato plucking is the norm, and in [[Folk music|folk]] and bluegrass music it is called the bass fiddle. In funk, blues and reggae it is often amplified.

Physics experiment demonstrating [[Wave–particle duality|wave–particle duality]] in light and matter. First described by [[Thomas Young (scientist)|Thomas Young]] in 1801 to support the wave theory of light, it sends light through two parallel slits, forming an interference pattern of bright and dark bands. Light still arrives at the screen as discrete particle hits, and the pattern no longer forms if detectors show which slit each [[Photon|photon]] passes through. Electrons, atoms and molecules show the same behavior. [[Richard Feynman]] said it contains "the only mystery" of quantum mechanics.

Mental state of indecision between two or more contradictory [[Proposition|propositions]], lying between belief and disbelief. It may involve uncertainty, distrust or lack of conviction about facts, actions, motives or decisions, and can delay or reject action out of concern for mistakes. In philosophy, Descartes used methodical doubt as a basic tool. In *On Certainty*, [[Ludwig Wittgenstein]] described how everyday use of the words doubt and certainty works. [[Søren Kierkegaard]] argued that to have belief is at the same time to have doubt. Doubt about the existence of God may lead to [[Agnosticism]] or [[Skepticism|skepticism]], or to acceptance of a religion, as in [[Pascal's wager]]. Doubt about some doctrines can produce [[Heresy|heresy]] and the splitting off of [[Sect|sects]].

Propeller-driven airliner and its military transport derivatives. One of the first airliners to profit from carrying only passengers, without mail subsidies, it carried around 90% of the world's [[Airline|airline]] flights in 1939. Civilian production ended in 1943 at 607 aircraft, but military versions, including the C-47 Skytrain, brought total production to over 16,000. It had a lasting effect on the airline industry from the 1930s through [[World War II]].

American engineer and inventor, a pioneer of [[Computer science|computer science]] and human–computer interaction. At the Augmentation Research Center at SRI International, he led development of the oN-Line System, which included the [[Computer mouse|computer mouse]], hypertext and bitmapped screens. These were demonstrated at "The Mother of All Demos" in 1968. He served as a radio and radar technician in the U.S. Navy in the [[Philippines]], then studied electrical engineering at the University of California, Berkeley, earning a [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]] in 1955. He won the 1997 ACM Turing Award, and in December 2000 [[Bill Clinton|President Bill Clinton]] awarded him the National Medal of Technology.

American general, Supreme Commander of Allied forces in the Southwest Pacific and of the occupation of Japan. He graduated first in his class at the U.S. Military Academy in 1903 and served with distinction in [[World War I]] on the [[Western Front (World War I)|Western Front]]. As chief of staff of the U.S. Army from 1930 to 1935, he was involved in the expulsion of Bonus Army protesters from [[Washington, D.C.]] in 1932. In World War II he escaped to Australia in March 1942 and in October 1944 led the campaign that liberated the Philippines. He accepted the [[Surrender of Japan|surrender of Japan]] in 1945 and oversaw the occupation until 1951. As head of the United Nations Command in the [[Korean War]], he suffered major defeats after China entered the war, and President [[Harry S. Truman]] removed him in April 1951.

[[Conifer]] species of the pine family, native to western [[North America]]. Despite its name, it is not a true [[Fir|fir]], [[Spruce|spruce]] or pine; its genus name, Pseudotsuga, means "false hemlock". It is the tallest tree in its family, reaching 20–100 metres (70–330 feet), and the largest coastal trees regularly live over 500 years, with the oldest over 1,300 years. Its thick, corky bark, up to 36 cm (14 in) on mature trees, makes it one of the most fire-resistant trees native to the [[Pacific Northwest]].

Genetic disorder, also called trisomy 21, caused by all or part of a third copy of chromosome 21. It is usually associated with developmental delays, mild to moderate [[Intellectual disability|intellectual disability]] and characteristic physical features, and it is the most common chromosomal abnormality, occurring in about 1 in 1,000 babies born worldwide. Incidence rises with maternal age, from less than 0.1% for 20-year-old mothers to 3% for those aged 45. Affected people have an increased risk of congenital heart disease, [[Epilepsy]], [[Leukemia]] and thyroid disease. There is no cure, but education and proper care improve quality of life, and life expectancy is around 50 to 60 years in the developed world. Rates of termination among [[Pregnancy|pregnancies]] diagnosed prenatally range from 50 to 85%, depending on maternal age, gestational age and race or ethnicity.

Receipt of data from a remote system over a [[Computer network|computer network]], such as a web, FTP or email server, as opposed to uploading. A download is also a file offered for, or obtained by, this transfer. Unlike [[Streaming media|streaming]], which uses data while transmission continues, downloading generally transfers entire files for local storage. Sites such as [[YouTube]] increasingly restrict users from saving streamed material. Legal action succeeded against the centralized network [[Napster]] but proved untenable against decentralized networks such as [[BitTorrent]].

British historical drama series created by Julian Fellowes, set on a fictional Yorkshire estate from 1912 to 1925. It follows the aristocratic Crawley family and their servants through events including the [[Sinking of the Titanic|sinking of the Titanic]], the [[Spanish flu]] pandemic and the [[Teapot Dome scandal]]. It first aired on ITV in 2010 and on [[PBS]] in the United States. Critics praised it, and [[Guinness World Records]] named it the most critically acclaimed English-language television series of 2011.

Broad-spectrum tetracycline-class [[Antibiotic|antibiotic]], sold under the brand names Vibramycin and Doryx. It treats infections caused by bacteria and some parasites, including [[Pneumonia|pneumonia]], acne, [[Chlamydia]] infections, [[Lyme disease]], cholera, [[Typhus]] and [[Syphilis]], and is sometimes used to prevent [[Malaria]]. It slows or kills bacteria by inhibiting protein production. Common side effects include diarrhea, nausea and increased sunburn risk. Patented in 1957, it came into commercial use in 1967 and is on the [[World Health Organization]]'s List of Essential Medicines.

American rapper, record producer and executive, co-founder of [[N.W.A]]. He founded Aftermath Entertainment, and his solo debut, *The Chronic* (1992), helped establish West Coast G-funk, a [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] subgenre built on [[Synthesizer|synthesizer]] sounds. He has won seven [[Grammy Awards]] and signed [[Eminem]] and [[50 Cent]]. In 1991 he pleaded no contest to assaulting television host Dee Barnes. Following widely publicized accusations of violence toward women, he issued a public apology in 2015.

Indian actor and singer in [[Kannada]] cinema, known as Annavru (elder brother). He appeared in over 205 films, including mythological and historical roles, and was the first Indian actor to play a role based on [[James Bond]] in a full-fledged manner. He received the Padma Bhushan in 1983 and the Dadasaheb Phalke Award in 1995. In 2000 he was kidnapped by the bandit Veerappan and held for 108 days.

American children's author, illustrator, animator and [[Cartoon|cartoonist]], whose full name was Theodor Seuss Geisel. He adopted the pen name at [[Dartmouth College]]. He began as an illustrator and cartoonist for magazines and advertisers, including a campaign for Flit and work for [[Standard Oil]]. During [[World War II]] he drew political cartoons and worked in the U.S. Army animation department. His more than 60 books, including *The Cat in the Hat* (1957) and *Green Eggs and Ham* (1960), have sold over 600 million copies. He received two Primetime Emmy Awards and a 1984 Pulitzer Prize special citation.

1964 political satire and black comedy film directed and co-written by [[Stanley Kubrick]]. Loosely based on Peter George's novel *Red Alert*, it parodies [[Cold War]] fears of nuclear war between the United States and the [[Soviet Union]]. [[Peter Sellers]] plays three characters. It was financed by [[Columbia Pictures]], and in 1989 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for the National Film Registry. It received four Academy Award nominations.

Species of [[Flowering plant|flowering plant]] native to tropical West Africa, also called snake plant and Saint George's sword. Its stiff leaves tolerate low light and little water, which makes it a popular houseplant. Its [[Stoma|stomata]] open only at night, limiting water loss through [[Evaporation|evaporation]]. A [[NASA]] Clean Air Study found it has potential to filter indoor air, but its rate is too slow for practical use. Like other members of the genus *Dracaena*, it yields bowstring hemp, a fiber once used to make bowstrings.

[[Constellation]] in the far northern sky, named for the [[Latin]] word for dragon. One of the 48 constellations listed by the 2nd-century Greek astronomer [[Ptolemy]], it remains one of the 88 modern constellations and is circumpolar from northern latitudes. Thuban (α Draconis) was the northern pole star from 3942 BC to 1793 BC. The brightest star is Gamma Draconis, an orange giant of magnitude 2.2 known as Etamin or Eltanin.

Traditional first legislator of [[Athens]] in [[Ancient Greece]]. He replaced oral law and blood feud with the [[Draconian constitution]], a written code enforced by a court, and set death as the penalty for most offenses. [[Solon]] repealed all of his laws except those on [[Homicide]]; an inscription from 409/8 BC refers to "the law of Draco about homicide". Some scholars consider him wholly or partly fictional. [[Plutarch]] reports that Draco said the lesser crimes deserved death and he had no greater penalty for the greater ones. The adjective draconian, meaning unusually harsh, derives from his name.

Written law code of [[Athens]] created by [[Draco (legislator)|Draco]] around 620 BC. Its laws were inscribed where literate citizens could read them, an early precursor to [[Rule of law|rule of law]] and Athenian democracy. It distinguished intentional from unintentional [[Homicide]] and made death the penalty for most offenses. The severity gave rise to the English word draconian, meaning excessively harsh. Only the homicide laws survived the reforms of Solon in the early 6th century BC.

[[Gothic fiction|Gothic horror]] novel by Irish author [[Bram Stoker]], first published in 1897. Told through letters, diary entries and newspaper articles, it follows English solicitor Jonathan Harker, who visits a [[Transylvania|Transylvanian]] nobleman, Count Dracula. The count, a [[Vampire|vampire]], moves to England, where a group led by Abraham Van Helsing hunts him. Stoker found the name in a history of [[Wallachia]] and Moldavia; scholars have proposed [[Vlad the Impaler]] and [[Elizabeth Báthory]] as inspirations, but recent scholarship disputes this. Because Stoker incorrectly filed the United States copyright, the novel is in the [[Public domain|public domain]] there. With over 700 appearances across media, Dracula was named the most portrayed literary character by the Guinness Book of World Records.

Retarding [[Force|force]] exerted by a fluid on an object moving through it, opposite to its direction of motion. Drag is proportional to [[Velocity|velocity]] at low speeds and to velocity squared at high speeds, a distinction measured by the [[Reynolds number]]. Form drag comes from pressure around a body and depends on its cross-sectional shape, while skin friction drag comes from [[Viscosity|viscous]] friction along the surface. [[Lift (force)|Lift]]-induced drag arises from [[Wing|wings]], and wave drag from shockwaves at high speeds; the wave drag of the [[Concorde]] prototype was reduced by 1.8% at Mach 2 by applying the area rule. For a top sprinter, overcoming drag can require 5% of their energy output.

Mythical, roughly serpentine creature found in the [[Folklore|folklore]] of cultures worldwide, often with wings and claws. Dragon-like creatures appear in ancient [[Mesopotamia]], and in [[Greek mythology]] drakontes were large serpents defeated by heroes or gods. In [[East Asia]], dragons were usually benevolent; Chinese dragons governed rain and water and became emblems of imperial power from the [[Han dynasty]] onward. In the Western tradition they became fire-breathing embodiments of evil. The English word comes from Old French, from Latin *draco*, meaning huge serpent, and from Ancient Greek *drákōn*. Modern fiction by [[J. R. R. Tolkien]], [[Ursula K. Le Guin]] and [[George R. R. Martin]] draws on these traditions.

Japanese media franchise created by [[Akira Toriyama]], based on a [[Manga|manga]] serialized in [[Weekly Shōnen Jump]] from 1984 to 1995. It follows the martial arts training and adventures of the Saiyan Son Goku, who seeks the seven Dragon Balls, orbs that summon a wish-granting dragon. The series draws on the 16th-century Chinese novel [[Journey to the West]] and Hong Kong martial arts films. Its 519 chapters were collected in 42 volumes, with 260 million copies sold worldwide. The [[Anime|anime]] series [[Dragon Ball Z]] was especially influential in popularizing Japanese animation in the [[Western world]]. The franchise also includes films, [[Action figure|action figures]], video games and trading card games.
